lessons.title: কিন্তু (kintu) — but
lessons.gloss: but — the first word in this book that can put two ideas against each other instead of side by side

needs: your eyes, because the lesson points at something written down
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your eyes, so it is not fully a driving lesson. You will want your eyes, because the lesson points at something written down. You can listen to all of it now and come back to the parts that need looking at once you have stopped.

segments.source: [PAUSE 2s]

segments.text: The chapter before this joined things and offered a choice between them. Neither joiner can disagree with anything.

segments.instruction: the two joiners of the last chapter — ār, bā
segments.source: [YOU RECALL: the two joiners of the last chapter — *ār*, *bā*]

segments.text: আমি ভালো, কিন্তু আমার চা নেই — āmi bhālo, kintu āmār chā nei — I am well, but I have no tea.

আর puts two things on the same side. কিন্তু (kintu) puts the second one against the first. It stands at the head of the clause it turns, after a comma in writing and after a small drop of the voice in speech.

কিন্তু (kintu) is Sanskrit kim-tu, and both halves are recoverable. Kim is "what" — the same ancient word standing behind কি, which chapter three taught. Tu is an old particle meaning "however". So but in Bengali is literally what-however, a shrug frozen into a conjunction.
Look at the middle of the written word: ন্ত is ন and ত fused by the mark chapter two taught for deleting the inherent vowel. Two letters, one shape, and no new letter to learn.

lessons.title: একমত (ekmôt) — of one mind
lessons.gloss: in agreement, of one mind — the word that lets a learner agree, and, with নই, disagree

segments.source: [PAUSE 2s]

segments.text: আচ্ছা has been in this book since chapter one and it says I see. It does not say I agree, and nothing else here does either.

segments.instruction: the word that turns a clause against the one before it — kintu
segments.source: [YOU RECALL: the word that turns a clause against the one before it — *kintu*]

segments.text: আমি একমত — āmi ekmôt — I agree.
আমি একমত নই — āmi ekmôt nôi — I do not agree.
The word is two words: এক, "one", which chapter twelve counted, and মত, "opinion". Of one mind. English builds the same picture out of Latin when it says unanimous — ūnus animus, one spirit.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: agreeing needs no verb, and disagreeing needs no new word

segments.text: আমি একমত (ekmôt) has no verb in it, like আমি ভালো before it — so it is denied the same way, with নই. The whole of agreement and disagreement in Bengali is now two words the reader already owns arranged in two orders.
Put কিন্তু (kintu) in front and you have the shape every conversation turns on: আমি একমত (ekmôt), কিন্তু (kintu) … — I agree, but …

segments.source: [PAUSE 1s]
[YOU SAY: *āmi ekmôt*]
[YOU SAY: *āmi ekmôt nôi*]

segments.instruction: the polite half-agreement — āmi ekmôt, kintu …
segments.source: [YOU SAY: the polite half-agreement — *āmi ekmôt, kintu …*]

segments.instruction: the one-word answers it can replace — hyã … nā
segments.source: [YOU SAY: the one-word answers it can replace — *hyã … nā*]
[PAUSE 3s]

segments.text: What are the two pieces of একমত (ekmôt)? (Ek, one, and môt, opinion.) Which negator denies it, and why that one? (নই — the sentence has no verb to put না after.) And which English word is built the same way out of Latin? (Unanimous.)
Source: Unicode Bengali chart.

lessons.title: কেননা (kenonā) — because
lessons.gloss: because — a reason word built out of "why" and "not", and the first way this book can explain anything

segments.source: [PAUSE 2s]

segments.text: Two lessons ago you could contradict somebody, and one lesson ago you could agree with them. Neither lets you say why.

segments.instruction: the two items before this one — kintu, ekmôt
segments.source: [YOU RECALL: the two items before this one — *kintu*, *ekmôt*]

segments.text: আমি একমত নই, কেননা আমার চা নেই — āmi ekmôt nôi, kenonā āmār chā nei — I do not agree, because I have no tea.
কেননা (kenonā) stands at the head of the reason, the way কিন্তু (kintu) stands at the head of the objection. The order is fixed: the claim first, the reason after it.

Pull কেননা (kenonā) apart and the negator of chapter twenty-seven falls out of it: কেন ("why") plus না ("not"). Bengali's word for because is a rhetorical question worn smooth — why not? — which is the same move English made in forasmuch as and inasmuch as before those went out of use.

Bengali writes another word here in everyday speech, kāraṇ, from Sanskrit kāraṇa, "cause". It is the commoner of the two and it needs a letter this book has not taught, so it is named in romanization and left for a script lesson. কেননা (kenonā) costs no new letters at all — every piece of it is already yours.

segments.text: What two words is কেননা (kenonā) built from? (কেন, why, and না, not.) Which comes first, the claim or the reason? (The claim — the reason follows it.) And which word does the same job at the head of an objection? (কিন্তু (kintu).)
Source: Unicode Bengali chart.

segments.text: Which of this chapter's three words heads an objection, and which heads a reason? (কিন্তু (kintu) the objection; কেননা (kenonā) the reason.) What is inside কেননা (kenonā) that chapter twenty-seven taught? (না.) And what would make the whole three-clause sentence a question? (A rising voice at the end, and nothing else.)
